title: Ferrule
pitch: Four relief charities, four separate databases, one shared queue. Ferrule is the WebMCP layer between origins: leased, policed, human approved, and every hop on a ledger that exports.
about_excerpt: Four relief charities, four separate databases, one shared queue. Ferrule is the WebMCP layer between origins: leased, policed, human approved, and every hop on a ledger that exports. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration In August 2022 a third of Pakistan went under water. My family is from Sindh. My uncle spent that month running between four places. A food store with rice and oil in it. A school that had become a shelter because it had a roof and a gate. A group of men with pickup trucks who would drive anywhere if you called them early enough. And a cold room, in the back of a pharmacy, holding the insulin for a whole district. Four organisations. Four sets of records. None of them could see the others. He held the entire thing together with a phone and a notebook. He wrote down who had what, who had asked for what, and who he had already promised it to. And he got things wrong, because anyone would. A family got sent to a shelter that had filled up an hour earlier. Boxes were double promised. Insulin sat in a cold room for two days because the person who needed to know it was there was on a different page of the notebook. Nobody in that story needed better software for their own organisation. The pantry knew its own stock perfectly well. The shelter knew its own beds. What was missing was the seam. The part between them. The thing my uncle was doing by hand with a biro. When I read the WebMCP spec, that is the gap I saw. Not another site publishing tools for itself, but the layer that lets a person and an agent work across four sites that will never, ever hand each other their data. Every organisation in that network had a reason to keep their own records. None of those reasons went away just because a flood arrived. So Ferrule is the notebook, rebuilt as software, with the agent doing the running around and the human still holding the pen for anything that costs something real. What it does Ferrule is a dispatch desk. Open it and you are looking at one queue that reaches across five independent websites, each on its own origin, each with its own data in its own browser storage. The four partner sites are real, usable sites. A volunteer can open the pantry and reserve a food box with no agent anywhere near it. What each one adds is a small set of WebMCP tools. Nineteen across the four of them. The Desk publishes seven verbs of its own and nothing else. intake_request , find_capacity , draft_plan , commit_plan , open_lease , close_lease , read_ledger . That is the whole surface any agent gets. No partner tool is ever callable directly, and there is no second path for a privileged caller, because there is no privileged caller. Here is what actually happens when the queue moves. A lease opens. Time boxed, scoped to a purpose, and it names exactly which partner tools it permits. Only once that lease is granted does the partner's own site mount into the Desk as a frame. It was not on the page a second earlier. When the lease closes, expires, or is revoked, the frame comes down and the tools it carried leave with it. The policy engine decides. Every hop is checked against a scope map before it travels. A refusal is a value with a sentence in it, never a thrown exception, so an agent reading the answer knows what happened and why. The run stops for a person. commit_plan is the one verb in the system that succeeds and goes nowhere. It answers with a status of awaiting_human_approval , an approval id, and a line telling the caller outright that none of its verbs continues from here. So a model reads that, reports the plan as raised, and stops, instead of looping or treating it as an error. What the human sees is the target origin, the tool, the arguments, the required scope, and a digest taken over the substance of the plan. Rename the plan and the digest holds. Change the origin, the tool, the arguments, or the order, and the approval is void. Then the write lands , and the partner's own page updates itself. Nothing is suggested for you to go and do by hand. Anything coming back is fenced. A value from a tool that declares untrusted content gets wrapped in a quarantine region, labelled as text written outside the Desk, and rendered as inert text. Data, never instruction. Every hop is recorded. Seventeen pinned fields per row, tab separated, byte stable, and it round trips: export the ledger and reimport it and you get the same bytes back. Who asked whom for what, the policy decision, the duration, and whether the approval came from the scripted run or from a model. There are three ways to drive it, and a judge needs nothing for any of them. Press Run the relief scenario . No key, no sign in, nothing to configure. A declared step list drives all seven verbs, crosses two origins, and stops at the approval. Open the agent controls and press Use the hosted endpoint, no key needed . Now a model picks the verbs and the order, and nobody wrote that order down. It opens its own lease, reads capacity, drafts a plan, and hits the same halt in front of the same person. Point a WebMCP extension or the Chrome DevTools WebMCP panel at the Desk. Seven declarations with schemas, read only hints, and a stated return shape on each one. There is also a topology view that draws the session as it happened, and an evidence page that lists sixteen security claims with a label on each saying what actually backs it. How we built it A pnpm monorepo, TypeScript end to end, deployed as six static sites plus one small endpoint. Front end. React 19 and Vite for all five product apps. Tailwind CSS 4 on the partner sites, because a partner site should look like a small charity built it. The Desk runs its own design system instead: a fixed eight by four grid that closes at 1280 by 800 with no page scroll, a four tier elevation ladder, and a set of pinned design tokens with a build check that fails if a value drifts off the four pixel base unit. The topology view is three.js through React Three Fiber. WebMCP. A platform wrapper sits over document.modelContext and is the only module in the entire repository allowed to name it. A syntax tree gate enforces that, rather than a code review convention. Under the wrapper is the vendored polyfill, pinned byte for byte, so the Desk behaves the same in a browser with native WebMCP and in one without. The broker. @ferrule/broker holds the frame host, the lease manager, the policy engine, the approval gate, the quarantine wrapper, and the ledger. It contains no React at all, which is deliberate: the lease state machine, the policy table, the digest, and the serialiser all run in a node test project against fakes, with no DOM anywhere near them. Origins. Every origin value lives once, in an origin registry. A build gate fails on a raw origin string literal anywhere else in apps/ or packages/ . All five product origins serve Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 on every path, and a gate fails the build if a site configuration drops the rule. The keyless agent. gateway/ is an Ope

My family is from Sindh, and my uncle spent that month between a food store, a school being used as a shelter, a group of men with pickup trucks, and a cold room holding the district's insulin. Four organizations, four separate records, none able to see the others. He held it together with a phone and a paper notebook, and he got things wrong because anyone would. That is the job I gave to an agent. Ferule is a dispatch desk. Four relief organizations keep their own sites and their own data, and one screen brokers an agent across all four with a person in the one step that spends something real. Seven verbs declared once on the desk's own document. Open a lease, read capacity, draft a plan, commit it, close. That is the whole surface an agent gets. No partner tool is ever called directly. A lease is a state machine, and it is the entire boundary. Requested, granted, mounted, then expired or revoked. Nothing crosses an origin without one. One hue per organization. Nothing else on the screen is colored, and five origins including one deliberately unkeyed. Every attempt lands in a ledger in order, refusals included. Before the desk, the pantry itself. This is a live site on its own origin with its own stock and its own browser storage, and a volunteer can use it with no agent anywhere in sight. What it adds is five web MCP tools declared at the foot of its own page. Four partners, 19 tools between them. No key, no sign-in, nothing to configure. Watch the seam. A lease opens on the pantry scoped to reading capacity and time boxed, and only now does the pantry's own site mount into this page as a frame. It was not here a second ago, and a tool that is not on the page cannot be called by anything. Capacity comes back, a second origin answers under its own lease, and every hop is already on the ledger. Then, the run stops. It stopped on purpose. The agent drafted a plan and called commit plan, and commit plan is the one verb here that succeeds and goes nowhere. How long it took, and where the approval came from. It exports and re-imports byte for byte. The same session drawn. Five origins, the lease on each, and the last few hops with the policy decision beside everyone. All of that was a declared step list. Here is the same surface with the model choosing. live_observation.first_impression: Ferrule Desk presents a relief-dispatch dashboard with a scenario button, a shared ledger, lease state-machine documentation, and an audit log.
live_observation.after_state: The dashboard and audit log remained unchanged, showing only the initial platform.boot entry; no scenario results appeared.
live_observation.notes: The shared-queue and ledger concepts were visible, but the central scenario action had no observable effect.
